# Foundational data frame subsetting
![](/images/subset_table.png){style="width:200px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"}

<u id='data_frame_tooltip'>__Data frames__</u> can be subset similar to <u id='vector_tooltip'>__vectors__</u>. 
As with <u id='vector_tooltip'>__vectors__</u> you can use `[]`. 
Additionally, `$` can be used to subset <u id='data_frame_tooltip'>__data frames__</u>.

Square brackets must be provided indexes for rows and for columns. 
The structure for this is `df[row,column]`. 
It is very useful to remember that R always wants rows first then columns second.

## Read in Parks biodiversity data frame
![](/images/biodiversity.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"}

To practice subsetting <u id='data_frame_tooltip'>__data frames__</u> with square brackets we will __read__ in a new file called [parks_biodiveristy.csv](https://neof-workshops.github.io/R_j4c0xh/downloads/parks_biodiveristy.csv). 
This contains the number of different species of various groups (Bird, Mammal, etc.) in US national parks.

```{r eval=FALSE}
#Read in the file
parks_df <- read.csv("parks_biodiveristy.csv", check.names = FALSE,
                             row.names = 1)
#View the resulting object
parks_df
#View its column names
colnames(parks_df)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="parks_biodiveristy.csv source"}
Original data can be found:

<https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/nationalparkservice/park-biodiversity>
:::

## Square bracket subsetting
![](/images/R_square_bracket.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"}

Now for some subset commands specifying the row/s then column/s with square brackets (`[]`).

```{r eval=FALSE}
#Scalar from the 1st row and 1st column
parks_df[1,1]
#Row names and column names can be used for indexing
#Scalar from the row called YOSE and the column called Amphibian
parks_df["YOSE","Amphibian"]
#More examples
parks_df[1:10,2]
parks_df[1:10,"State"]
parks_df[3,2:4]
parks_df["SAGU",2]
parks_df[1:10,"Bird"]
parks_df[c(1,3,5,6),c("Bird","Fish")]
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Rows then columns
A quick reminder that it is always rows then columns in square brackets.

`df[row,column]`
:::

## Subsetted object

As you can see in the above set of code the structure of the resulting subsetted object is dependant on how it was subsetted.
It may be a <u id='scalar_tooltip'>__scalar__</u>, <u id='vector_tooltip'>__vector__</u>, or <u id='data_frame_tooltip'>__data frame__</u>. 

Below describes what structure your resulting subsetted object will be based on the subsetting.

- <u id='scalar_tooltip'>__Scalar__</u>: 
    - Indexing to get a single value by choosing one row and one column
    - E.g. `parks_df[1,1]`
- <u id='vector_tooltip'>__Vector__</u>:
    - Indexing so you get multiple values from one column
    - This occurs as each column is in essence a <u id='vector_tooltip'>__vector__</u>
    - E.g. `parks_df[1:10,2]`
- <u id='data_frame_tooltip'>__Data frame__</u>:
    - Indexing so you get multiple values from a row or multiple rows
    - Subsetting a <u id='data_frame_tooltip'>__data frame__</u> like this provides you with a <u id='data_frame_tooltip'>__data frame__</u>
    - E.g. `parks_df[3,2:4]` or `parks_df[3:4,2:4]`
